brief.topic: A Steady Pour and an Unsteady Rise

s01: A steady pour can make a water level rise at an unsteady pace.
In a bowl that widens upward, the rise gradually slows.
Imagine a cone-shaped vessel with its point below.
Near the bottom, a little water fills a tall narrow space.
Higher up, the same added volume must spread across a wider surface.
A larger surface needs more water for the same rise.
For a perfect cone, radius grows in proportion to water depth.
Volume therefore grows with the cube of that depth.
At half the vessel height, the water occupies only one eighth of its capacity.
Half the height is not half the water.
This is geometry under a steady inflow, with no water escaping.
The point and smooth sides are idealizations.
Now place a straight-sided vessel beside it, with the same total capacity and height.
Pour equal amounts into both at the same steady rate.
In the straight vessel, equal volumes give equal rises.
When each is half full by volume, the cone is already about four fifths of the way up.
The water keeps its volume; the shape changes how we see its progress.

scenes.narration:
A steady pour can make a water level rise at an unsteady pace. In a bowl that widens upward, the rise gradually slows.

Imagine a cone-shaped vessel with its point below. Near the bottom, a little water fills a tall narrow space. Higher up, the same added volume must spread across a wider surface. A larger surface needs more water for the same rise.

For a perfect cone, radius grows in proportion to water depth. Volume therefore grows with the cube of that depth. At half the vessel height, the water occupies only one eighth of its capacity. Half the height is not half the water.

This is geometry under a steady inflow, with no water escaping. The point and smooth sides are idealizations.

Now place a straight-sided vessel beside it, with the same total capacity and height. Pour equal amounts into both at the same steady rate. In the straight vessel, equal volumes give equal rises. When each is half full by volume, the cone is already about four fifths of the way up. The water keeps its volume; the shape changes how we see its progress.
